expectedText:
CHILD SUPPORT AGREEMENT
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF PARENTS AND SUPPORT AMOUNT
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, as the parents of Riley Lee (date of birth: April 3, 2019), state that they intend the following child support arrangement: Jordan Alex Lee agreeing to pay Morgan Casey Lee the amount of $850 per month, beginning October 1, 2026, until the arrangement ends or is modified as described in this document.

STATEWIDE GUIDELINE AMOUNT IS PRESUMPTIVELY CORRECT
Under California's child support statute, the amount produced by the statewide uniform guideline formula is presumed to be the correct amount of child support to be ordered. That presumption is rebuttable and affects the burden of proof — a party seeking a different amount carries the burden of showing, by admissible evidence, that applying the formula would be unjust or inappropriate given the specific circumstances. Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee acknowledge that a support figure agreed between parents is not automatically the "correct" amount in the way this statute defines that term; it is an amount the parents propose regarding support for Riley Lee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The amount of child support established by the formula provided in subdivision (a) of Section 4055 is presumed to be the correct amount of child support to be ordered. (b) The presumption of subdivision (a) is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof and may be rebutted by admissible evidence showing that application of the formula would be unjust or inappropriate in the particular case, consistent with the principles set forth in Section 4053, because one or more of the following factors is found to be applicable by a preponderance of the evidence, and the court states in writing or on the record the information required in subdivision (a) of Section 4056:"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4057(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the presumptive-correctness rule and its rebuttable burden (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4057.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a guideline-based child support system frames the relationship between an agreed number and a legally "correct" number — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. Whether a guideline formula exists at all, whether it is rebuttable, and what burden of proof applies are all jurisdiction-specific and vary state to state. This is a single statutory section (§ 4057(a)-(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

ENUMERATED PRINCIPLES BEHIND THE GUIDELINE
California's child support statute states that the courts must adhere to a specific, enumerated list of principles when implementing the guideline, including: a parent's first and principal obligation is to support the parent's minor children according to the parent's circumstances and station in life; both parents are mutually responsible for the support of their children; each parent should pay for the support of the children according to the parent's ability; the guideline seeks to place the interests of children as the state's top priority; children should share in the standard of living of both parents, and child support may therefore appropriately improve the standard of living of the custodial household; the financial needs of the children should be met through private financial resources as much as possible; and the guideline is intended to be presumptively correct in all cases, with departures below the guideline formula reserved for special circumstances.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "In implementing the statewide uniform guideline, the courts shall adhere to the following principles: (a) A parent's first and principal obligation is to support the parent's minor children according to the parent's circumstances and station in life. (b) Both parents are mutually responsible for the support of their children. (c) The guideline takes into account each parent's actual income and level of responsibility for the children. (d) Each parent should pay for the support of the children according to the parent's ability. (e) The guideline seeks to place the interests of children as the state's top priority. (f) Children should share in the standard of living of both parents. Child support may therefore appropriately improve the standard of living of the custodial household to improve the lives of the children. (g) Child support orders in cases in which both parents have high levels of responsibility for the children should reflect the increased costs of raising the children in two homes and should minimize significant disparities in the children's living standards in the two homes. (h) The financial needs of the children should be met through private financial resources as much as possible. (i) It is presumed that a parent having primary physical responsibility for the children contributes a significant portion of available resources for the support of the children. (j) The guideline seeks to encourage fair and efficient settlements of conflicts between parents and seeks to minimize the need for litigation. (k) The guideline is intended to be presumptively correct in all cases, and only under special circumstances should child support orders fall below the child support mandated by the guideline formula. (l) Child support orders shall ensure that children actually receive fair, timely, and sufficient support reflecting the state's high standard of living and high costs of raising children compared to other states."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4053 (California Legislative Information text), the enumerated statutory principles (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4053.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a real, specific, enumerated set of policy principles underlies a guideline child support system — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. Whether any such principles are codified, and what they say, varies by state. This is a single statutory section (§ 4053); no additional independent source was found for this.

THE STATEWIDE GUIDELINE FORMULA
California's guideline formula for calculating child support is codified as an algebraic equation: CS = K[HN - (H%)(TN)]. In the formula, CS is the child support amount; K is the share of both parents' combined income allocated to child support; HN is the higher-earning parent's net monthly disposable income; H% is the approximate percentage of time the higher-earning parent has (or will have) primary physical responsibility for the children, compared to the other parent; and TN is the total net monthly disposable income of both parents combined. The statute further specifies that K itself is not a fixed number — it is calculated from a formula that varies with H% and with the parents' combined net monthly income, using a bracketed schedule set out in the statute. Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee may reference their own net incomes and time-sharing percentages for Riley Lee as informational inputs, without this document performing or certifying a guideline calculation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The statewide uniform guideline for determining child support orders is as follows: CS = K[HN - (H%)(TN)]. (b) (1) The components of the formula are as follows: (A) CS = child support amount. (B) K = amount of both parents' income to be allocated for child support as set forth in paragraph (3). (C) HN = high earner's net monthly disposable income. (D) H% = approximate percentage of time that the high earner has or will have primary physical responsibility for the children compared to the other parent. In cases in which parents have different time-sharing arrangements for different children, H% equals the average of the approximate percentages of time the high earner parent spends with each child. (E) TN = total net monthly disposable income of both parties."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4055(a)-(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), the formula and its defined variables (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4055.)
  "K (amount of both parents' income allocated for child support) equals one plus H% (if H% is less than or equal to 50 percent) or two minus H% (if H% is greater than 50 percent) times the following fraction: Total Net Disposable Income Per Month K $0–2,900 0.165 + TN/82,857 $2,901–5,000 0.131 + TN/42,149 $5,001–10,000 0.250 $10,001–15,000 0.10 + 1,499/TN Over $15,000 0.12 + 1,200/TN"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4055(b)(3) (California Legislative Information text), the K-factor income-band schedule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4055.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that an income-based guideline formula with this specific algebraic structure exists and is codified in exact numeric detail — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter, and not a representation that this formula applies outside California. The formula, its defined variables, and its K-factor schedule are all jurisdiction-specific; most states use an entirely different model (for example, an "income shares" model rather than California's percentage-of-income model), so neither the equation nor its coefficients transfer to another state's guideline. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 4055) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

LOW-INCOME ADJUSTMENT
California's guideline statute includes a specific low-income adjustment mechanism. Where the support-paying parent's net disposable monthly income is less than the amount of monthly gross income earned from full-time minimum wage, there is a rebuttable presumption that parent is entitled to a low-income adjustment reducing the guideline amount, calculated by a statutory fraction. That presumption can be rebutted by evidence that applying the lowest permitted support amount would be unjust and inappropriate in the particular case, considering the statute's stated principles and the impact of the adjustment on both parents' net incomes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "In all cases in which the net disposable income per month of the obligor is less than the amount of monthly gross income earned from full-time minimum wage, established by Section 1182.12 of the Labor Code, at 40 hours per week, 52 weeks per year, there is a rebuttable presumption that the obligor is entitled to a low-income adjustment. The presumption may be rebutted by evidence showing that the application of the lowest amount of child support permitted pursuant to this paragraph would be unjust and inappropriate in the particular case. In determining whether the presumption is rebutted, the court shall consider the principles provided in Section 4053, and the impact of the contemplated adjustment on the respective net incomes of the obligor and the obligee."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4055(b)(7) (California Legislative Information text), the low-income adjustment presumption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4055.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a guideline formula can include a specific, codified low-income adjustment mechanism, rather than assuming one exists — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. This draws on the same statutory section as the guideline-formula clause above (§ 4055); no additional independent source was found for the low-income adjustment itself. Whether a low-income adjustment exists, and how it is calculated, is jurisdiction-specific and varies by state.

ENUMERATED GROUNDS FOR DEPARTING FROM THE GUIDELINE
California's statute lists specific, enumerated factors that can support a departure from the guideline formula amount, including: the parties have stipulated to a different amount under the statute's stipulation provision; sale of the family residence is deferred and the rental value of the residence where the children reside exceeds the mortgage, insurance, and property tax payments; the parent ordered to pay support has an extraordinarily high income and the formula amount would exceed the children's needs; a party is not contributing to the children's needs at a level commensurate with that party's custodial time; a support obligor qualifies for the statute's low-income adjustment and the formula amount (after that adjustment) would still exceed 50 percent of the obligor's net disposable income; and other special circumstances, including different time-sharing arrangements for different children, a large disparity in housing-cost burden between parents with substantially equal timeshare, a child's special medical or other needs, or a child found to have more than two parents.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(1) The parties have stipulated to a different amount of child support under subdivision (a) of Section 4065. (2) The sale of the family residence is deferred pursuant to Chapter 8 (commencing with Section 3800) of Part 1 and the rental value of the family residence where the children reside exceeds the mortgage payments, homeowner's insurance, and property taxes. The amount of any adjustment pursuant to this paragraph shall not be greater than the excess amount. (3) The parent being ordered to pay child support has an extraordinarily high income and the amount determined under the formula would exceed the needs of the children. (4) A party is not contributing to the needs of the children at a level commensurate with that party's custodial time. (5) A support obligor qualifies for the low-income adjustment pursuant to paragraph (7) of subdivision (b) of Section 4055 and the amount of child support established by the formula exceeds 50 percent of the support obligor's net disposable income as defined in Section 4059 after application of the low-income adjustment. The amount of any adjustment pursuant to this paragraph shall not be greater than the amount exceeding 50 percent of the support obligor's net disposable income. (6) Application of the formula would be unjust or inappropriate due to special circumstances in the particular case. These special circumstances include, but are not limited to, the following: (A) Cases in which the parents have different time-sharing arrangements for different children. (B) Cases in which both parents have substantially equal time-sharing of the children and one parent has a much lower or higher percentage of income used for housing than the other parent. (C) Cases in which the children have special medical or other needs that could require child support that would be greater than the formula amount. (D) Cases in which a child is found to have more than two parents."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4057(b)(1)-(6) (California Legislative Information text), the enumerated departure grounds (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4057.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that departure from a guideline formula is limited to a specific, enumerated list of grounds rather than open-ended negotiation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. This draws on the same statutory section as the presumptive-correctness clause above (§ 4057); no additional independent source was found for the departure list itself. What circumstances (if any) justify departing from a guideline amount is jurisdiction-specific and varies by state.

CONDITIONS FOR A STIPULATED BELOW-GUIDELINE AMOUNT
California's statute allows parties to stipulate to a child support amount, subject to court approval, but sets specific conditions before a court may approve a stipulated amount that is below the guideline formula amount. The statute requires the parties to declare that: they are fully informed of their rights concerning child support; the order is being agreed to without coercion or duress; the agreement is in the best interests of the children involved; the needs of the children will be adequately met by the stipulated amount; and the right to support has not been assigned to the county and no public assistance application is pending.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Unless prohibited by applicable federal law, the parties may stipulate to a child support amount subject to approval of the court. However, the court shall not approve a stipulated agreement for child support below the guideline formula amount unless the parties declare all of the following: (1) They are fully informed of their rights concerning child support. (2) The order is being agreed to without coercion or duress. (3) The agreement is in the best interests of the children involved. (4) The needs of the children will be adequately met by the stipulated amount. (5) The right to support has not been assigned to the county pursuant to Section 11477 of the Welfare and Institutions Code and no public assistance application is pending."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4065(a) (California Legislative Information text), the conditions for a stipulated below-guideline amount (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4065.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a below-guideline agreed amount is conditioned on a specific, enumerated set of declarations rather than free negotiation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter, and not a certification that these conditions have been met here. Whether a jurisdiction permits stipulated below-guideline support at all, and on what conditions, is jurisdiction-specific and varies by state. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 4065(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

MANDATORY VS. DISCRETIONARY ADD-ON EXPENSES
California's statute distinguishes mandatory from discretionary additional child support amounts. It requires courts to order, as additional child support: childcare costs actually incurred that are related to employment or to reasonably necessary education or training for employment skills (unless already included in the guideline calculation), and reasonable uninsured health care costs for the children. Separately, it authorizes but does not require courts to order, as additional child support: costs related to the educational or other special needs of the children, and travel expenses for visitation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) The court shall order the following as additional child support: (1) Childcare costs, if those expenses are actually incurred, related to employment or to reasonably necessary education or training for employment skills, as described in Section 4063, unless those costs are specifically included in the guideline calculation itself. (2) The reasonable uninsured health care costs for the children as provided in Section 4063. (b) The court may order the following as additional child support: (1) Costs related to the educational or other special needs of the children. (2) Travel expenses for visitation."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4062(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the mandatory/discretionary add-on distinction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4062.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a guideline system can distinguish mandatory from discretionary add-on expense categories, and how one state actually draws that line — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. Which expense categories (if any) are mandatory versus discretionary is jurisdiction-specific and varies by state. This is a single statutory section (§ 4062(a)-(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

ADD-ON EXPENSE ALLOCATION
The parents allocate the following categories of additional expenses for Riley Lee as follows: childcare/employment-related care costs — Split equally; uninsured health care costs — Split equally; educational or special-needs costs — Split equally; travel expenses for visitation — Each parent pays their own. This schedule is a blank-fill allocation reference only and states no legal claim about which of these categories any jurisdiction treats as mandatory or discretionary.

DURATION OF THE SUPPORT OBLIGATION
California's statute establishes that the parental duty to support a minor child continues as to an unmarried child who has turned 18, is a full-time high school student, and is not self-supporting, until the child completes the 12th grade or turns 19, whichever occurs first; a child who has a physician-documented medical condition preventing full-time school attendance is excused from the full-time-student requirement without ending the support duty on that basis alone.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Subject to this division, the father and mother of a minor child have an equal responsibility to support their child in the manner suitable to the child's circumstances."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3900 (California Legislative Information text), the general parental support obligation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3900.)
  "(1) The duty of support imposed by Section 3900 continues as to an unmarried child who has attained 18 years of age, is a full-time high school student, unless excused pursuant to paragraph (2), and who is not self-supporting, until the time the child completes the 12th grade or attains 19 years of age, whichever occurs first. (2) A child is excused from the requirement to be a full-time high school student for purposes of paragraph (1) if the child has a medical condition documented by a physician that prevents full-time school attendance."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3901(a) (California Legislative Information text), the age-18-plus-high-school-student extension and its medical exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3901.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a parental child support duty can be tied by statute to a specific age plus a school-enrollment condition, rather than a flat age cutoff — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. The age, school-enrollment condition, and any medical exception are all jurisdiction-specific and vary by state.

SUPPORT ORDERS INCLUDE AN EARNINGS ASSIGNMENT
California's statute provides that when a court orders a party to pay support, or modifies a support amount, the court's order must include an earnings assignment order directing the paying parent's employer to pay the support obligee directly, in an amount sufficient to cover both the ongoing support amount and any amount ordered toward liquidating arrears. The statute states this earnings assignment order is effective and enforceable even without the employer's name, address, or other identifying information on file at the time it issues.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) When the court orders a party to pay an amount for support or orders a modification of the amount of support to be paid, the court shall include in its order an earnings assignment order for support that orders the employer of the obligor to pay to the obligee that portion of the obligor's earnings due or to become due in the future as will be sufficient to pay an amount to cover both of the following: (1) The amount ordered by the court for support. (2) An amount which shall be ordered by the court to be paid toward the liquidation of any arrearage. (b) An earnings assignment order for support shall be issued, and shall be effective and enforceable pursuant to Section 5231, notwithstanding the absence of the name, address, or other identifying information regarding the obligor's employer."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 5230(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the mandatory earnings assignment order (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=5230.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a court-ordered support obligation can carry an automatic wage/earnings withholding mechanism directed at the paying parent's employer — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. Whether an earnings assignment is automatic, optional, or unavailable, and how it is triggered, is jurisdiction-specific and varies by state; this clause also does not describe how withholding would apply to a private agreement that has not been entered as a court order. This is a single statutory section (§ 5230(a)-(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

SIGNATURE BLOCK
Signed by Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

Signed by Morgan Casey Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

citations.quote: (1) The parties have stipulated to a different amount of child support under subdivision (a) of Section 4065. (2) The sale of the family residence is deferred pursuant to Chapter 8 (commencing with Section 3800) of Part 1 and the rental value of the family residence where the children reside exceeds the mortgage payments, homeowner's insurance, and property taxes. The amount of any adjustment pursuant to this paragraph shall not be greater than the excess amount. (3) The parent being ordered to pay child support has an extraordinarily high income and the amount determined under the formula would exceed the needs of the children. (4) A party is not contributing to the needs of the children at a level commensurate with that party's custodial time. (5) A support obligor qualifies for the low-income adjustment pursuant to paragraph (7) of subdivision (b) of Section 4055 and the amount of child support established by the formula exceeds 50 percent of the support obligor's net disposable income as defined in Section 4059 after application of the low-income adjustment. The amount of any adjustment pursuant to this paragraph shall not be greater than the amount exceeding 50 percent of the support obligor's net disposable income. (6) Application of the formula would be unjust or inappropriate due to special circumstances in the particular case. These special circumstances include, but are not limited to, the following: (A) Cases in which the parents have different time-sharing arrangements for different children. (B) Cases in which both parents have substantially equal time-sharing of the children and one parent has a much lower or higher percentage of income used for housing than the other parent. (C) Cases in which the children have special medical or other needs that could require child support that would be greater than the formula amount. (D) Cases in which a child is found to have more than two parents.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that departure from a guideline formula is limited to a specific, enumerated list of grounds rather than open-ended negotiation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. This draws on the same statutory section as the presumptive-correctness clause above (§ 4057); no additional independent source was found for the departure list itself. What circumstances (if any) justify departing from a guideline amount is jurisdiction-specific and varies by state.

expectedJSON.body: California's statute allows parties to stipulate to a child support amount, subject to court approval, but sets specific conditions before a court may approve a stipulated amount that is below the guideline formula amount. The statute requires the parties to declare that: they are fully informed of their rights concerning child support; the order is being agreed to without coercion or duress; the agreement is in the best interests of the children involved; the needs of the children will be adequately met by the stipulated amount; and the right to support has not been assigned to the county and no public assistance application is pending.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4065(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the conditions for a stipulated below-guideline amount
citations.quote: Unless prohibited by applicable federal law, the parties may stipulate to a child support amount subject to approval of the court. However, the court shall not approve a stipulated agreement for child support below the guideline formula amount unless the parties declare all of the following: (1) They are fully informed of their rights concerning child support. (2) The order is being agreed to without coercion or duress. (3) The agreement is in the best interests of the children involved. (4) The needs of the children will be adequately met by the stipulated amount. (5) The right to support has not been assigned to the county pursuant to Section 11477 of the Welfare and Institutions Code and no public assistance application is pending.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a below-guideline agreed amount is conditioned on a specific, enumerated set of declarations rather than free negotiation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter, and not a certification that these conditions have been met here. Whether a jurisdiction permits stipulated below-guideline support at all, and on what conditions, is jurisdiction-specific and varies by state. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 4065(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: California's statute distinguishes mandatory from discretionary additional child support amounts. It requires courts to order, as additional child support: childcare costs actually incurred that are related to employment or to reasonably necessary education or training for employment skills (unless already included in the guideline calculation), and reasonable uninsured health care costs for the children. Separately, it authorizes but does not require courts to order, as additional child support: costs related to the educational or other special needs of the children, and travel expenses for visitation.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4062(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) The court shall order the following as additional child support: (1) Childcare costs, if those expenses are actually incurred, related to employment or to reasonably necessary education or training for employment skills, as described in Section 4063, unless those costs are specifically included in the guideline calculation itself. (2) The reasonable uninsured health care costs for the children as provided in Section 4063. (b) The court may order the following as additional child support: (1) Costs related to the educational or other special needs of the children. (2) Travel expenses for visitation.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a guideline system can distinguish mandatory from discretionary add-on expense categories, and how one state actually draws that line — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. Which expense categories (if any) are mandatory versus discretionary is jurisdiction-specific and varies by state. This is a single statutory section (§ 4062(a)-(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: The parents allocate the following categories of additional expenses for Riley Lee as follows: childcare/employment-related care costs — Split equally; uninsured health care costs — Split equally; educational or special-needs costs — Split equally; travel expenses for visitation — Each parent pays their own. This schedule is a blank-fill allocation reference only and states no legal claim about which of these categories any jurisdiction treats as mandatory or discretionary.

California's statute establishes that the parental duty to support a minor child continues as to an unmarried child who has turned 18, is a full-time high school student, and is not self-supporting, until the child completes the 12th grade or turns 19, whichever occurs first; a child who has a physician-documented medical condition preventing full-time school attendance is excused from the full-time-student requirement without ending the support duty on that basis alone.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3900 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Subject to this division, the father and mother of a minor child have an equal responsibility to support their child in the manner suitable to the child's circumstances.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3901(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the age-18-plus-high-school-student extension and its medical exception
citations.quote: (1) The duty of support imposed by Section 3900 continues as to an unmarried child who has attained 18 years of age, is a full-time high school student, unless excused pursuant to paragraph (2), and who is not self-supporting, until the time the child completes the 12th grade or attains 19 years of age, whichever occurs first. (2) A child is excused from the requirement to be a full-time high school student for purposes of paragraph (1) if the child has a medical condition documented by a physician that prevents full-time school attendance.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a parental child support duty can be tied by statute to a specific age plus a school-enrollment condition, rather than a flat age cutoff — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. The age, school-enrollment condition, and any medical exception are all jurisdiction-specific and vary by state.

expectedJSON.body: California's statute provides that when a court orders a party to pay support, or modifies a support amount, the court's order must include an earnings assignment order directing the paying parent's employer to pay the support obligee directly, in an amount sufficient to cover both the ongoing support amount and any amount ordered toward liquidating arrears. The statute states this earnings assignment order is effective and enforceable even without the employer's name, address, or other identifying information on file at the time it issues.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 5230(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) When the court orders a party to pay an amount for support or orders a modification of the amount of support to be paid, the court shall include in its order an earnings assignment order for support that orders the employer of the obligor to pay to the obligee that portion of the obligor's earnings due or to become due in the future as will be sufficient to pay an amount to cover both of the following: (1) The amount ordered by the court for support. (2) An amount which shall be ordered by the court to be paid toward the liquidation of any arrearage. (b) An earnings assignment order for support shall be issued, and shall be effective and enforceable pursuant to Section 5231, notwithstanding the absence of the name, address, or other identifying information regarding the obligor's employer.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a court-ordered support obligation can carry an automatic wage/earnings withholding mechanism directed at the paying parent's employer — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. Whether an earnings assignment is automatic, optional, or unavailable, and how it is triggered, is jurisdiction-specific and varies by state; this clause also does not describe how withholding would apply to a private agreement that has not been entered as a court order. This is a single statutory section (§ 5230(a)-(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.
